<!-- head-1: body_md -->
proving propositions are indicated by the keywords \verb|       | and \verb|     |. There is no semantic difference between these keywords; the distinction exists solely for humans to distinguish ``more important'' and ``less important'' theorems.
    \item
<!-- end head-1 -->
<!-- head-2: body_md -->
constructing non-propositional data such as functions are indicated by the keywords \verb|   |, \verb|      |, \verb|         | and \verb|         |. A \verb|   | needs to be unfolded in a proof by tactics (described below) to access its definition, while an \verb|      | does not. \verb|         | is the most general way of defining new \textit{types} in Lean; \verb|         | defines a non-recursive type, akin to \verb|      |s in C and C++.
    \item \textbf{Type classes} are indicated by the keyword \verb|     | and instantiated by \verb|        |. Redhill does not define any type classes or instances because none of its results need to be \textit{ad hoc} polymorphic, but larger projects like \verb|       | use them extensively \cite{instance-abuse}.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end head-2 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
A tuple $(a_1,\dots,a_n)$ satisfies the strong subsum condition if for any tuple $(b_1,\dots,b_n)$ with $b_i\in\{-1,0,1\}$ and $\sum_i b_ia_i=0$, $b_1=\dots=b_k$. This implies the subsum condition, where $b_i\in\{0,1\}$.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
Given a tuple $(a_1,\dots,a_n)$, a sub-tuple $(a_{i_1},\dots,a_{i_k})$ is a subsum block if for any tuple $(b_1,\dots,b_n)$ with $b_i\in\{-1,0,1\}$ and $\sum_i b_ia_i=0$, $b_{i_1}=\dots=b_{i_k}$.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
If the tuple obtained by summing the elements of a subsum block into one new element satisfies \verb|         |, so does the original tuple.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Expand the definition of \verb|         | for the original and reduced tuples.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
Given a tuple $(a_1,\dots,a_n,c_1,\dots,c_m)$, $(c_1,\dots,c_m)$ is a subsum block if for all non-constant tuples $(b_1,\dots,b_m)$ with $b_j\in\{-1,0,1\}$ we have
    \begin{equation*}
        \sum_{i=1}^n|a_i|<\left|\sum_{j=1}^m b_jc_j\right|.
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Consider a sign-weighted sum of the entire tuple where $a_i$ has weight $d_i\in\{-1,0,1\}$:
    \begin{equation*}
        \sum_{i=1}^n d_ia_i+\sum_{j=1}^m b_jc_j
    \end{equation*}
    By the triangle inequality the first sum's magnitude cannot exceed $\sum_{i=1}^n|a_i|$, so the second sum cannot exactly cancel out the first sum \textit{unless $(b_1,\dots,b_m)$ is a constant tuple}, which is the definition of $(c_1,\dots,c_m)$ being a subsum block.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
Given a tuple $(a_1,\dots,a_n,x,y)$, $(x,y)$ is a subsum block if the following inequalities hold:
    \begin{equation*}
        \sum_{i=1}^n|a_i|<|x|\qquad\sum_{i=1}^n|a_i|<|y|\qquad xy\le0
    \end{equation*}
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
There are six possible ways to associate different signs to $x$ and $y$:
    \begin{equation*}
        (0,1)\qquad(0,-1)\qquad(1,0)\qquad(-1,0)\qquad(1,-1)\qquad(-1,1)
    \end{equation*}
    It is easy to check that the strict inequality condition in \verb|                | is satisfied in each case. The last two cases satisfy the inequality because $xy\le0$ implies $|x-y|=|y-x|=|x|+|y|$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
Let $m$ and $s$ be natural numbers with $0<m\le s$ and $p_1,\dots,p_n$ be primes with $s<p_1$ and $2p_{i-1}<p_i$ for $i=2,\dots,n$. Then \verb|        | $(p_1,\dots,p_n,m,-(m+\sum_{i=1}^n p_i))$ satisfies \verb|         |.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
We proceed by induction on $n$. At $n=0$, \verb|        | is $(m,-m)$, which is easily seen to satisfy \verb|         | because $m\ne0$.

    Now suppose the proposition is true for $n=k$. \verb|        | at $n=k+1$ is then
    \begin{equation*}
        \left(p_1,\dots,p_k,p_{k+1},m,-\left(m+\sum_{i=1}^{k+1} p_i\right)\right).
    \end{equation*}
    
    The third-last and last elements of this tuple form a subsum block by \verb|                     |, because another induction argument on the given inequalities shows that
    \begin{equation*}
        m+\sum_{i=1}^k p_i<p_{k+1}.
    \end{equation*}

    Summing the subsum block into one element and permuting gives \verb|        | at $n=k$, which satisfies \verb|         | by the inductive hypothesis. The inductive step follows by \verb|                   |.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
Given two natural numbers $u$ and $m$, there exist two other natural numbers $v$ and $w$ such that $w=u+v$, $m<v$, $w$ is odd and $k$ does not divide $v$ or $w$ if $3\le k\le m$. If in addition $0<u\le m$, $v$ and $w$ can be chosen to be coprime.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
We choose $v=m+1+s$ and $w=m+1+u+s$, where $s$ is a natural number ``shift'' to be determined. They clearly satisfy $w=u+v$ and $m<v$, so we need only consider the non-divisibility conditions for $s$.

    Given any integer $p\ge3$, the pigeonhole principle applied to residues modulo $p$ provides a number $s_p$ with
    \begin{align*}
        m+1+s_p&\not\equiv0\bmod p\\
        m+1+u+s_p&\not\equiv0\bmod p.
    \end{align*}

    When $p=4$, simple casework provides a number $s_4$ with
    \begin{align*}
        m+1+s_4&\not\equiv0\bmod 4\\
        m+1+u+s_4&\not\equiv0\bmod\mathbf2.
    \end{align*}

    The Chinese remainder theorem (\href{https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/9e6b3aac99b624d10c84653ab9c5357283b9b3b8/Mathlib/Data/Nat/ChineseRemainder.lean#L165}{\Verb|Nat.chineseRemainderOfFinset|}) then provides a number $s$ satisfying $s\equiv s_4\bmod 4$ and $s\equiv s_p\bmod p$ for all primes $3\le p\le m$. Since every number in $[3,m]$ is divisible by one of these moduli, using this $s$ satisfies the non-divisibility conditions.

    To show $v$ and $w$ are coprime when $0<u\le m$, suppose $p$ is a common prime factor. $p\ne2$ since $w$ is odd, so $p>m$ because neither $v$ nor $w$ is divisible by any number in $[3,m]$. But $p\mid u$ since $w=u+v$, so $p\le u$, contradicting $u\le m$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
Let $m$ and $s$ be natural numbers with $0<m\le s$ and $p_1,\dots,p_n$ be primes with $s<p_1$ and $2p_{i-1}<p_i$ for $i=2,\dots,n$. Let $B$ be another natural number such that $m+\sum_{i=1}^n p_i\le B$ and let $v$ and $w$ be the corresponding fields in a \lstinline[mathescape]{VWPair $(m+\sum_{i=1}^n p_i)$ $B$}.

    Then \verb|     | $(p_1,\dots,p_n,v,-w,m)$ satisfies \verb|         |.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
$v$ and $-w$ form a subsum block by \verb|                     |. It is clear that $m+\sum_{i=1}^n p_i>0$; expanding the properties of $v$ and $w$ gives
    \begin{align*}
        \mathtt{eq\_add}&:\ w=m+\sum_{i=1}^n p_i+v\\
        \mathtt{m\_lt\_v}&:\ B<v
    \end{align*}
    so $0<m+\sum_{i=1}^n p_i<v<w$, the strict inequality conditions in $\verb|                     |$ are met and $v\cdot-w<0$. Summing the subsum block into one element and permuting gives \verb|        |, so \verb|     | satisfies \verb|         | by \verb|                   | and \verb|                  |.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
If $|x|\ge y$, \verb|   | satisfies \verb|         |.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Knowing \textit{a priori} that $1530\le y$, we prove these estimates for the polynomial head's entries:
    \begin{align*}
        21|x|^4\le\,&|(x-1)^5|\\
        &|10(x^2+1)^2|\le20|x|^4\\
        21|x|^4\le\,&|-(x+1)^5|
    \end{align*}

    Then we show that for $b_1,b_2,b_3\in\{-1,0,1\}$ not all equal,
    \begin{equation*}
        y\le|b_1\cdot(x-1)^5+b_2\cdot10(x^2+1)^2+b_3\cdot-(x+1)^5|.
    \end{equation*}

    The sum of magnitudes of \verb|   |'s remaining entries, $\sum_{i=1}^n p_i+v+w$, is strictly less than $y$, so the polynomial head's entries form a subsum block by \verb|                |. Summing this block into one element gives an instance of \verb|     | satisfying \verb|         |; the result follows by \verb|                   |.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
For all odd $n\ge5$ and all finsets $F$ of natural numbers not containing $0$, $1$, $2$, $5$ or $10$, \verb|                    | has quality at least $5/3$. Ramaekers's conjecture is thus false for these values of $n$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
For all $n\ge6$ and all finsets $F$ of natural numbers not containing $0$, $1$ or $2$, \verb|                    | has quality at least $5/4$. Ramaekers's conjecture is thus false for these values of $n$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Recall that entries outside the polynomial head are constant, so they only contribute a constant factor $C$ to the upper bound on the radical of the product of \verb|   |'s entries:
    \begin{align*}
        \operatorname{rad}(C\cdot(x^2+10y^3)^2\cdot(10y-1)x^4\cdot(x-y)^5\cdot(x+y)^5)&\le C'\cdot(x^2+10y^3)\cdot\operatorname{rad}(x)\cdot(x-y)\cdot(x+y)\\
        &=C'\cdot(x^2+10y^3)\cdot\operatorname{rad}((y+1)^{h!})\cdot(x^2-y^2)\\
        &=C'\cdot(x^2+10y^3)\cdot\operatorname{rad}(y+1)\cdot(x^2-y^2)\\
        &=C''\cdot(x^2+10y^3)\cdot(x^2-y^2)
\end{align*}
where $C'$ and $C''$ are constants. This is an upper bound of degree $4$, while \verb|   |'s maximum absolute value is $(x+y)^5$ of degree $5$. Applying the argument at the beginning of section \ref{disproof} gives the result.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\verb|                 | has quality at least $9/8$, so Ramaekers's conjecture is false for $n=4$.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
\href{https://github.com/Parcly-Taxel/Redhill/blob/arxiv-fixed/Redhill/Four.lean#L31-L37}{The construction} is broadly similar to those that we encountered in section \ref{disproof}, in that a tuple of polynomials is evaluated at specific points:
\begin{gather*}
    (a_0:=u^9, a_1:=(8-u)^5(u^2+20u+280)^2, a_2:=-105(2u-3)^6,\\
    a_3:=130032u^4 + 10728480u^3 - 202978980u^2 + 1238324220u - 2568934655)
\end{gather*}

It is an algebraic identity that $a_0+a_1+a_2+a_3=0$.
\begin{lstlisting}
                                                                                            
                           
                                                                                     

                                                                                    
                                   
                                 
              
                                                 
                               
            
\end{lstlisting}

For each pair $X,Y$ of irreducible polynomials (including $-105$ in $a_2$) that are factors of different $a_i$, there exist two other polynomials $A,B$ and a constant $c$ such that $AX+BY=c$ with no common factor among all of $A,B,c$, so $X$ and $Y$ are coprime if they are coprime modulo $c$. Substituting $u=19$ makes all such pairs coprime modulo their corresponding $c$, and we can easily show that $u$ is coprime to $u^2+20u+280$ if $u\equiv19\bmod70$. Thus \verb|   | has pairwise coprime entries if $u\equiv19\bmod M$, where
\begin{equation*}
    M=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot13\cdot23\cdot41\cdot103\cdot113\cdot127\cdot149
    \cdot197\cdot439\cdot1249\cdot395119\cdot649541\cdot399635598557777987
\end{equation*}
is the least common multiple of all moduli $c$.

When $u\ge19$, the inequalities $1<a_3<-a_2<a_0$ and $a_3<-a_1<a_0$ hold. It is then a simple matter to show that \verb|   | satisfies the subsum condition (\textit{not} \verb|         |) by considering each possible proper subset and calling the \verb|     | tactic to prove that it cannot sum to $0$.

We have proved that \verb|   | is in \verb|                 | if $u\ge19$ and $u\equiv19\bmod M$. An infinite sequence of evaluation points that always satisfies these conditions is $u_k=(35(2M+1)^k+3)/2$. To finish the proof of the lower bound on quality, we derive an upper bound of degree $8$ on $\operatorname{rad}(a_0a_1a_2a_3)$:
\begin{align*}
    \operatorname{rad}(a_0a_1a_2a_3)&\le 105\cdot u_k\cdot(8-u_k)\cdot(u_k^2+20u_k+280)\cdot\operatorname{rad}(2u_k-3)\cdot a_3\\
    &=105\cdot u_k\cdot(8-u_k)\cdot(u_k^2+20u_k+280)\cdot\operatorname{rad}(35(2M+1)^k)\cdot a_3\\
    &=C\cdot u_k\cdot(8-u_k)\cdot(u_k^2+20u_k+280)\cdot\underbrace{a_3}_{\text{degree 4}}
\end{align*}
where $C$ is a constant. The inequalities between the $a_i$ used to prove the subsum condition also show that the maximum absolute value is $a_0=u^9$. Once again, applying the argument at the beginning of section \ref{disproof} gives the result.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
